lesson.title: Averaging the Evidence: The Sample Mean
lesson.summary: The sample mean is the arithmetic average of the values in a sample, and it serves as the standard statistic used to estimate an unknown population mean.
lesson.body:
Just as categorical data is often summarized by a proportion, numeric data is most often summarized by a mean. When a population has some true average value, a fixed but usually unknown parameter denoted mu (for instance, the true average commute time of every employee at a company), we cannot compute mu directly without measuring every individual in the population. Instead, we take a sample and compute the sample mean, which is used as an estimate of mu.

The sample mean, written x-bar, is calculated by adding up every value in the sample and dividing by the sample size n. If a sample contains values x1, x2, up through xn, then x-bar equals the sum of those values divided by n. Because x-bar is calculated entirely from the sample data, it is a statistic, in exactly the same sense that the sample proportion p-hat is a statistic: it describes the sample, not the population, and it will vary depending on which individuals happened to be selected.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a teacher randomly selects 5 exam scores from a large class: 82, 91, 76, 88, and 95. The sample mean is x-bar = (82 + 91 + 76 + 88 + 95) / 5. Adding those five scores: 82 + 91 = 173, plus 76 gives 249, plus 88 gives 337, plus 95 gives 432. Dividing by 5 gives x-bar = 432 / 5 = 86.4. That value, 86.4, summarizes this particular sample of five scores and serves as an estimate of the true mean score across the entire class, mu, which we do not know unless every student's score is included.

As with the sample proportion, it helps to keep straight what is fixed and what varies. The population mean mu does not depend on which students happen to be sampled, it is a single fixed number describing the entire class. The sample mean x-bar depends entirely on the five scores selected, and a different sample of five students would almost certainly produce a different x-bar, maybe 84.2 or 89.6 instead of 86.4. That variability from sample to sample is exactly what the sampling distribution of the mean, covered next, describes.
